date_label: Correspondence from c. 1897–98 (after Opals); pursuit, Paris visit, and Italian holiday c. 1901; contact sustained after Custance's 1902 marriage
summary: After Opals (1897) Barney opened the acquaintance with a letter of admiration, wooed Custance with love poems, and invited her to Paris, where Custance also befriended Barney's former lover Renée Vivien; around 1901 Barney and Custance holidayed together in Italy while Custance was simultaneously conducting her courtship with Douglas. Accounts of the Barney–Vivien–Custance ménage are contradictory: Barney's memoir says she tried to persuade Custance to join a Sapphic community at Mytilene (stymied by Vivien's jealousy), and per McDermott she 'supposedly envisaged marrying Douglas as a way of inducing Olive to live with her too'. Custance kept up contact with Barney after returning to London in 1901 and marrying in 1902, and Custance verse survives among Barney's papers.

sources.quote: Shortly after this, she received a letter of admiration from Natalie Barney (1876-1972), a Parisian salon hostess who would become notorious for her openly lesbian poetry published in 1900 as Quelques Portraits-Sonnets de Femmes. Barney wooed Custance with several love poems and invited her to Paris, where Custance also befriended the symbolist poet Renée Vivien (1877-1909), one of Barney’s former lovers.
sources.context: Parker's Y90s biography; 'this' is the publication of Custance's Opals (1897), so the correspondence opens c. 1897–98. The same paragraph continues: 'Accounts of this ménage are often contradictory; Barney's autobiography Souvenirs Indiscrets (1960) states that she tried to persuade Custance to join her and Vivien in recreating a Sapphic community at Mytilene, but the endeavour was stymied by Vivien's jealousy.'
sources.supports: Barney initiated the acquaintance after Opals; wooing with love poems; the Paris invitation.

sources.quote: Custance sustained contact with both Barney and Vivien after she moved back to London in 1901, and her diaries and poems suggest she continued to be attracted to and inspired by women.
sources.context: Parker's Y90s biography, close of the Barney/Vivien paragraph.
sources.supports: Custance back in London 1901; the connection continued past the liaison; diaries/poems as evidence of her attraction to women.

sources.quote: she was also being pursued by yet another admirer, this time a woman, and an American. Nathalie Barney, a wealthy heiress and salon hostess in Paris saw herself as a latter day Sappho. … Soon after, on holiday in Italy with Barney, Olive annoyed her friend by spending the whole time gazing at a photo of a classical statue of Antinoüs whom, she said, reminded her of her new pen friend, Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.context: McDermott's profile, in the passage on Custance at 27 (born Feb. 1874, hence c. 1901), concurrent with the Douglas courtship; 'Nathalie' is McDermott's spelling. He then prints Custance's Antinoüs poem with the note that its typed MS survives 'among the papers of Natalie Barney at the Sorbonne' — a poem is evidence of address, not of acts.
sources.supports: Independent secondary source frames Barney as pursuer; a joint Italian holiday c. 1901; the Douglas courtship running inside the Barney liaison.

sources.quote: Another arena in which Custance’s name arises is that of lesbian biography, in which her rumoured entanglements with Natalie Barney and Renée Vivien in Paris attract passing interest (Wickes 1977: 58-60; Souhami 2004: 56-51).
sources.context: Parker's peer-reviewed 2011 article, opening page; read in the Loughborough repository accepted manuscript, whose pagination differs from the journal printing (22.2-3 (2011), 220-40). The page span '56-51' is as printed in the am. Full citations per the am reference list: Wickes, The Amazon of Letters (London: W. H. Allen, 1977); Souhami, Wild Girls (London: Orion Books, 2004).
sources.supports: Status of the claim in scholarship: the Barney (and Vivien) entanglements are 'rumoured', treated in lesbian biography at the cited loci.
sources.citation_provenance: Loughborough repository (accepted manuscript; figshare file 16939550), p. 1

sources.quote: *. For I would dance to make you smile, and sing / Of those who with some sweet mad sin have played, / And how Love walks with delicate feet afraid / Twixt maid and maid.*
sources.context: Custance's verse answering Barney's first letter to her. Barney had written to the author of Opale enclosing two of her own books; 'Opale répondit avec feu' - Opale answered with fire. **Barney never names Custance in this memoir**: she is 'Opale' throughout, after her first collection, and the surname Custance does not occur in the volume. The suspension points opening the quotation are Barney's, marking that she quotes from mid-poem; slashes mark line breaks; endnote marker 3 omitted as typography. Custance's English is printed in italics inside the French text.
sources.supports: Custance's own words to Barney at the opening of the courtship - participant testimony from the other side, and unambiguous as to register.
sources.citation_provenance: The chapter 'RENÉE VIVIEN' runs PDF pp. 22-84. The memoir gives no source for Custance's lines and no location for the letter that carried them. One lead, not a location: writing of two Milosz letters Barney says she entrusted them to the Bibliothèque Doucet "ainsi que beaucoup d'autres" - much of her correspondence went there, and the Fonds Natalie Clifford Barney is at the Bibliothèque littéraire Jacques Doucet. Whether this letter is among it, the book does not say.
sources.speaker: Olive Custance, letter to Natalie Barney

sources.quote: Sa première visite fut pour nous et m'enchanta, car lorsque j'embrassai cette fraîche jeune fille, éblouissante de couleur et vibrante de poésie, j'eus l'impression d'étreindre la campagne anglaise.
sources.translation: Her first visit was to us and enchanted me, for when I kissed this fresh young girl, dazzling with colour and vibrant with poetry, I had the impression of embracing the English countryside.
sources.translation_note: Barney uses two different verbs of embrace and the sentence turns on the difference: 'j'embrassai' of the girl is rendered 'kissed', keeping 'embracing' for 'd'etreindre' of the countryside, so that the figure still lands on the same word in English as in French.
sources.context: Custance's first visit to Barney and Vivien in Paris. The same page records Vivien refusing to go to Custance's tea - 'Je n'irai pas' ('I shall not go') - on the grounds that Custance's gaiety and appearance were unworthy of her verse; Barney reads deeper antagonism under it.
sources.supports: The participant's own account of the physical opening of the liaison, and of Vivien's jealousy of it.
sources.citation_provenance: The chapter 'RENÉE VIVIEN' runs PDF pp. 22-84.
sources.speaker: Natalie Clifford Barney

sources.quote: Loin de suivre l'exemple de cette passion qui la rendait infidèle au professeur B.C., Opale et moi grelottions de fièvre — non de celle que nous avions espéré éprouver, mais d'une malaria qui nous laissa, tout le temps de notre séjour, affaiblies, au point de ne pouvoir quitter nos lits jumelés. Opale fit accrocher au-dessus de son lit de convalescence une photographie d'Antinoüs, qui la faisait rêver à Lord Alfred Douglas. … Cependant, comme elle tenait à conserver son poète, elle ourdit le plan de m'envoyer Lord Alfred aux Etats-Unis, dans l'espoir qu'un mariage blanc entre lui et moi permettrait de tout concilier.
sources.context: Venice, where Barney had taken Custance to have her to herself. Barney's wry 'not the fever we had hoped to feel' is the participant's own acknowledgement of what the trip was for. The elision drops one sentence explaining that Custance could not marry Douglas because she was already engaged elsewhere. This passage is also the origin of the Barney-Douglas thread: Custance's scheme to send Douglas to Barney in America and settle everything with a mariage blanc. Endnote marker 5 omitted as typography.
sources.supports: The liaison at its height, named obliquely but unmistakably by the participant; and Custance's own manoeuvre to keep both Barney and Douglas.
sources.citation_provenance: The chapter 'RENÉE VIVIEN' runs PDF pp. 22-84.
sources.speaker: Natalie Clifford Barney
sources.translation: Far from following the example of that passion which made her unfaithful to Professor B.C., Opale and I shivered with fever — not the fever we had hoped to feel, but a malaria that left us weakened for the whole of our stay, to the point of being unable to leave our twin beds. Opale had a photograph of Antinous hung above her convalescent's bed, which set her dreaming of Lord Alfred Douglas. … However, since she was set on keeping her poet, she hatched a plan to send Lord Alfred to me in the United States, in the hope that a mariage blanc between him and me would settle everything.
sources.translation_note: 'Mariage blanc' is left in French: it means a marriage never consummated, and there is no English phrase that carries it as exactly.

sources.quote: When Olive reported this unexpected development, Natalie said, “Tell him I'm in love with you.” … Needless to say, she was much more attracted to Olive, especially after an evening they spent bathed in moonlight and poetry. One evening was not enough, however; Natalie wanted to be alone with Olive for a longer time. So when Mrs. Custance and Freddy returned to England, Olive and Natalie went off to Venice, accompanied by the inevitable chaperone … Olive hung the photograph of her lover over her bed. This was none other than Lord Alfred Douglas.
sources.context: Wickes on Custance's spring 1901 visit to Paris. 'Freddy' is Frederick Manners-Sutton, heir to the Viscount Canterbury, who had fallen for Barney himself. The Venice trip ended with both women ill with malaria.
sources.supports: Biographer account of the Barney–Custance entanglement.

sources.quote: Natalie was enchanted with Olive – her wonderful complexion, her vibrant poetry. Renée Vivien was morbidly jealous, and Olive was in love with ‘Bosie’, Lord Alfred Douglas. The Bosie connection fired Natalie's desire for Olive.
sources.context: Souhami on the same 1901 visit. Note the causal claim in the last sentence - Souhami has Barney's interest in Custance partly driven by Custance's attachment to Douglas.
sources.supports: Biographer account of the Barney–Custance liaison.

null_findings.finding: Souvenirs indiscrets does not describe a plan to bring Custance and Vivien together in a Sapphic community at Mytilene. At PDF p. 42 Barney proposes to Vivien a group of poetesses 'comme celles qui entouraient Sapho à Mytilène' - Mytilene is a simile - and they act on it by inviting Custance to join them in Paris, rue Alphonse-de-Neuville. The actual Mytilene journey (PDF pp. 64-66) is Barney and Vivien alone, years later, and Custance is not mentioned in it. The Paris plan failed: Vivien refused to socialise with Custance at all (PDF p. 48). Barney never names Custance in the volume - she is 'Opale' throughout.
